title: Die Stadt wurde gerettet
subtitle: The passive, now and in the past, and three ways to say one thing
words.intro: Passau sits where three rivers meet, and every few years they come into town together. On the old town hall the marks of the floods run up the wall, with dates, higher than your head.

grammar[0].fact: The newspaper is the natural home of the German passive: nobody is to blame, and there’s only so much room. Officials love it for the same reasons. Read a local paper’s front page, and count the *wurde*. Then count the people named.

document.intro: A real wall in Passau. A hand points to the water level, and it’s far over your head. Each plaque is a past flood. The top one is 500 years old, and it spells everything differently: *wassergüss* is a flood.
document.fact: Marks like these are all along German rivers. They are old-fashioned insurance advice: if you’re buying a house, look at the wall first. Some of the highest marks are above the first-floor windows.

reading.intro: The river has risen in a small town in Bavaria, and Lena’s cousin Vroni works for the local newspaper. She has two versions of the same story: the one she has written for Saturday’s edition, and what she tells Lena on the phone.
reading.photos[0].caption: Sandsäcke an der Straße: Sie wurden in der Nacht gebracht.
reading.photos[1].caption: Passau, Juni 2013: Hier wurde das Wasser zur Straße.
reading.fact: German has a word that means something like this: *Nachbarschaftshilfe*, neighbourly help. After the floods of 2002 and 2013, tens of thousands of people came with shovels, many organised through social media and many unasked. The *Bundeswehr* and the *THW*, a largely volunteer civil protection agency, were there too.
